title: Squashing the competition: How one Illinois town became ‘pumpkin capital of the world’
text:
Squashing the competition: How one Illinois town became ‘pumpkin capital of the world’
Morton, Illinois, makes enough puree for 72 million pumpkin pies a year. Our reporter went to learn the town’s secrets – and to capture a slice of life.
Hunting for the heart of American pumpkin is not without its hazards. As I slow my rental car for a glimpse of the activity in a field off one stick-straight central Illinois highway, a white pickup truck roars up behind me, its driver leaning on the horn.
The two-lane road cuts through flat pumpkin fields, flanked by steep drainage ditches. I can’t pull over. And, admittedly, I am traveling way below the 55 mph speed limit. But as I speed up in the name of self-preservation, I also find what I am looking for: evidence of the season’s final pumpkin roundup.
It’s the end of October. Go time. A combine is kicking up dust as it scoops up pale-orange squash from neat rows and launches them through the air into the back of a trailer. These very pumpkins, my sources tell me, will be trucked, washed, chopped, steamed, pureed, and pressed into steel cans within four hours.
For Thanksgiving, the Monitor takes a closer look at the ingredients in pumpkin pie, including pumpkins, eggs, and flour, to discover what stories they might hold. In Morton, Illinois, our reporter captures a slice of life from the town that produces most of the world’s canned pumpkin today.
I’m in Morton, Illinois, the “pumpkin capital of the world” and home to the Nestlé-owned Libby’s processing plant. The facility turns locally grown squash into the vast majority of the country’s canned pumpkin, producing enough to fill 72 million pies each year. As the label says, one can of Libby’s is 100% pumpkin.
I want to see how it happens.
It will not be easy.
Central Illinois has a formula for pumpkins that’s hard to beat: rich prairie soils, a long growing season, and generations of family farmers who have worked to ensure the land is properly tended for fast-growing pumpkin vines. According to the Department of Agriculture, Illinois produced 96% of the country’s processed pumpkin last year – that’s 230,969 tons. And Libby’s has had a corner on that market for nearly 100 years. According to widely cited industry estimates, the brand with the ubiquitous orange label produces about 85% of the global supply of canned pumpkin.
All its pumpkins are grown here, within an 80-mile radius of Morton, a village of about 17,500.
In New England, where I live, agritourism is part of harvest season. Small farms offer tours, lodging, festivals, and hands-on experiences to supplement income. But what does it mean to live in the town surrounded by fields that supply most of America’s canned pumpkins? I came to Morton hoping to find out.
This, it would turn out, was no trip to pick out a jack-o’-lantern from a pumpkin patch. This was Big Ag.
Team pumpkin spirit
Still, when it comes to life in the pumpkin capital, residents brim with pumpkin pride. This is the heartbeat of America’s heartland, where 30 Christian churches serve Morton and the surrounding area. Images of the squash adorn everything from city welcome signs to business logos to front-porch pillows. It also appears as larger-than-life forms, such as a children’s slide in the center of town, and pumpkin mascots Libby and Gourdy, who regularly visit schools and nursing homes.
Some 1,500 volunteers run a four-day pumpkin festival in September, which offers every imaginable kind of pumpkin food: pancakes, muffins, chili, soup, fudge, and highly sought-after pumpkin ice cream. Orange becomes the town uniform.
“It is very much like wearing team spirit colors,” says Kim Litwiller, executive director of the Morton Chamber of Commerce, which organizes the festival. “The village as a whole has definitely grabbed hold of the uniqueness of having a pumpkin factory right here.”
And what about that factory? From August to November, I’m told it runs 24/7.
I want to go. I want to watch pumpkins being crushed, smell the puree, and hear the cans clatter along a conveyor belt.
Growing pumpkins in Illinois
Pumpkins arrived in Illinois from Kentucky as seeds in the pocket of Elijah Dickinson in 1835. Those seeds would eventually come to be known as Dickinson pumpkins – tawny, thick-skinned squash prized for their dense and sweet orange flesh. By 1925, the Dickinson Canning Company, which already operated two other canneries in the state processing corn, peas, string beans, and pumpkins, had begun operations in Morton. In 1929, Chicago canning company Libby, McNeill & Libby bought the Dickinson plants. It also obtained the exclusive rights to the Dickinson pumpkin cultivar and soon began contracting with local farmers to grow it. By 1972, the Morton plant focused exclusively on pumpkins. Six years later, Gov. James R. Thompson proclaimed Morton the “pumpkin capital of the world.”
It’s hard to make a plan to watch the pumpkin harvest because Libby’s controls the throttle of when and where it happens. But David Uhlman, a third-generation pumpkin farmer, calls me with a time and place. I follow him early one morning to his field in nearby Tremont, Illinois. We stand in grass heavy with dew and watch a tractor with a low-angled bar roll his pumpkins off the vines into neat rows. This is the first step before one of Libby’s pumpkin combines arrives to scoop them up.
Mr. Uhlman’s family has been growing pumpkins since his grandfather immigrated from Germany and settled in the area in the late 1920s. The pumpkins evolved over that time, cultivated for thicker skins and rounder shapes to make them easier to transport. Pumpkins aren’t his only crop. He also grows corn, soybeans, wheat, and some alfalfa hay for cattle. Each year, Libby’s signs new contracts with area farmers based on its existing inventory and provides the seed, he explains. Its field scouts make decisions about pesticides and fungicides during the growing season. After harvest, Libby’s requires farmers to rest pumpkin fields for about four years. (Libby’s did not comment for this story, but I did receive a fact sheet that highlighted the company’s regenerative agricultural practices, its zero-waste disposal facility, and water recycling process.)
“My job is fertility of the ground,” says Mr. Uhlman. “I care enough to prepare my soil so that it grows a healthy pumpkin.” This is a good year. So far, no killing frost and not too much rain. Mr. Uhlman has grown about 100 acres of pumpkins and expects to produce around 20 tons per acre.
“It is very rewarding to look across and see that many pumpkins out there,” he says, noting there are no empty spots in the rows. “This is one crop I know is farm-to-table. It goes right from here to the cannery.”
But Mr. Uhlman says he won’t be eating pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving.
“It’s not a texture or a flavor that I care for,” he admits. “My reward is growing them. I’ll sit down to ice cream.”
More than pumpkin pie
When pressed, other residents in Morton also admit that, when it comes to pumpkin, they prefer to think outside the pie plate.
“There are so many better ways for pumpkin to shine truly in a baked good,” says Rachel Berchtold, who owns and manages the local Eli’s Coffee, one of several local bakeries, with her husband, Weston. They sell an array of pumpkin pastries this time of year, including pumpkin coffee cake with a coffee cream cheese swirl throughout, an oatmeal streusel, and brown butter icing. “I love that so much more than a piece of gluey pumpkin pie,” she says.
But there is one person in town who “bleeds orange”: Mayor Jeff Kaufman. The public official once raised $75,000 to hire a faith-based independent movie company to film “Baking Up Love,” a Hallmark-style movie filmed in town and centered on a pumpkin pie contest. The picture did not win critical accolades.
Each year, Mayor Kaufman walks the pumpkin festival’s parade route, tossing out 300 pounds of candy. He cuts a pumpkin vine stretched across the main stage to officially open the festival. On this day, he greets me enthusiastically in his office at town hall and shows me a trophy he won in a boat race by kneeling and paddling in an enormous, carved-out pumpkin. For the next hour, he details his plans – many, many plans – to keep pumpkins front and center.
“It is a reunion,” says Mr. Kaufman of the yearly festival. “You see your kids, grandkids, and you see everybody else’s kids that come back. Everybody wants to see everybody. ... It’s a good excuse, but they all want their pumpkin pie, pumpkin ice cream.”
The festival is only four days, but the pumpkin harvesters keep emptying the fields as the tallgrass prairies of Illinois turn into a sea of ocher, amber, and gold right up until November.
“It is such a marker of the season change to watch the interstate fill up with 18-wheelers full of pumpkins rolling into Morton,” says Ms. Berchtold. Her shop is so close to the Libby’s plant that, when the wind blows just right on warm days, “it is not pleasant,” she says. “It is just part of the air around here.”
But has anyone seen the inside of the plant?
Few residents have been inside Libby’s within recent decades. The Nestlé-run plant no longer offers tours to school groups or to a curious journalist who calls asking to see inside. I stand on a sliver of sidewalk in front of the plant, peering through the chain-link fence to watch a man in a hardhat and fluorescent vest hose down freshly arrived field pumpkins filling a trailer tipped up at a 45-degree angle. Things are moving fast.
“It’s like Willy Wonka over there,” says Ms. Litwiller, the chamber of commerce director. “If you get to go on a tour, it’s like winning a golden ticket.”
I did not, dear reader, get that ticket.
But I came away with something else: the mayor’s wife’s grandmother’s prized pie recipe and, with it, a bit of shared pumpkin warmth.
